# RFC: Workflow-Driven Anonymization for Agent Builder

**Status:** Draft **Author:** Jon Wålstedt **Date:** 2026-04-28 

**Supersedes:** the deprecated profile-based anonymization \- to be removed:

- `x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/anonymization` (plugin)  
- `x-pack/platform/packages/shared/ai-infra/anonymization-common` (package)  
- `x-pack/platform/packages/shared/ai-infra/anonymization-ui` (package)

---

## 1\. Overview

### 1.1 Vision

Anonymization is an **invisible cross-cutting concern**. Agents, tools, and consumers know nothing about it. A user authors a Workflow whose ID is registered in Agent Builder's pre-prompt workflow list; AB invokes that workflow synchronously from inside its `beforeAgent` hook handler and stores the resulting token map on the per-round `RunContext`. The runner then applies the map transparently at the LLM I/O boundary. The LLM never sees real PII; the user, storage, and allowlisted tools never see tokens.

### 1.2 Goal

Replace the deprecated profile-heavy system with a lightweight solution that:

* Uses **NER \+ RegEx** for detection \- no per-target profile lookup, no field-level lineage, no Stack Management UI.

* Plugs into **only the existing** Agent Builder lifecycle hooks (`beforeAgent`, `beforeToolCall`, `afterToolCall`) \- no new public lifecycle is added.

* Configures rules **by-value in Workflow YAML** \- the Workflow is the only configuration surface.

* Holds token maps in **request-scoped memory only** \- no `.kibana-anonymization-replacements` index, no encrypted-at-rest storage. Multi-turn consistency is achieved via HMAC-deterministic tokens with one stable per-conversation salt (§5.2).

* **NER runs within a trusted boundary** \- detection must not use the same external LLM that the data is being protected from (§4.2).

* Automatically **injects a token-explanation instruction** into the system prompt when anonymization is active, so the LLM handles tokens correctly without hallucinating their values (§3.7).

* Defines a **merge strategy** for when multiple workflows are configured for `beforeAgent` and return overlapping token maps (§3.6).

* Ships as **two reusable platform primitives** in `kbn-anonymization`: the `ai.pii` workflow step (any workflow can call it) and an `AnonymizingChatModel` decorator (any plugin using `@kbn/inference-langchain` composes it where it constructs the model). Agent Builder is one consumer that wires them up transparently for chat agents; other GenAI surfaces (notably `elastic_assistant` in Security Solution) adopt the same primitives by the same composition pattern. There is no automatic "free for everyone" injection \- the decorator is a regular langchain decorator, applied at construction time.

### 1.3 Non-goals (this round)

* Field-level masking and ES|QL data lineage (out of scope per Slack consensus).  
* A dedicated UI for managing anonymization rules (rules live in Workflow YAML).  
* Storing message history in anonymized form (storage stays as-is with real values; anonymization is an LLM-edge concern only).  
* Adding `afterAgent` or any other new public lifecycle hook (§3.2 explains why we don't need one).

---

## 2\. User Journeys

Two illustrative journeys ground the rest of the document: one for the role *configuring* anonymization, one for the role *using* an agent that has anonymization configured. The second journey is deliberately uneventful \- that's the whole point.

### 2.1 Configuration Workflow (Administrator Role)

**Context.** An organization is rolling out internal AI agents in Kibana. Compliance has flagged that messages may contain PII (employee names, internal IDs) that should not reach external LLM providers. A security administrator owns getting anonymization configured for the space.

**Steps.**

1. **Author the workflow.** The administrator opens the Workflows app in Kibana and creates a new workflow (e.g., "Org PII Anonymization"). A step is added from the palette under **AI → PII Anonymizer** (`ai.pii`). The step is a registered `BaseStepDefinition` (same shape as `ai.classify`, `ai.summarize`, etc., per `src/platform/plugins/shared/workflows_extensions/common/steps/ai/`); the editor renders a configuration form derived from its Zod input schema, so each option below is a labelled field with type-correct affordances rather than a freeform YAML snippet.  
     
2. **Pick entity classes from the canonical vocabulary.** The `entities` field is a multi-select populated from `kbn-anonymization`'s `ANONYMIZATION_ENTITY_CLASSES`. The administrator selects `PER, ORG, LOC, EMAIL, IP, HOST_NAME, USER_NAME`. Only valid classes appear \- there is no way to type a class that doesn't exist.  
     
3. **Decide whether to use NER.** The `ner_deployment_id` field is a selector listing the cluster's deployed ML trained models \- NER is *not* an Elasticsearch `_inference` task type (the supported values are `text_embedding`, `sparse_embedding`, `rerank`, `completion`, `chat_completion`); detection is performed via the trained models API at `_ml/trained_models/{deployment_id}/_infer`, the same surface the deprecated implementation already uses (`execute_ner_rule.ts:135`). The editor populates the dropdown from the ML trained models registry. By default the cluster ships Elastic's CoNLL-03 DistilBERT model on ES ML nodes \- fully local, no data leaves the cluster \- and the administrator picks it from the dropdown. (If the cluster has no ML nodes, or graceful degradation is desired when ML capacity is unavailable, the field is left empty \- the step then runs in regex-only mode.)  
     
4. **Add custom regex rules.** For organization-specific identifiers \- e.g., internal employee IDs of the form `EMP-12345` and resource IDs of the form `ACME-RES-A1B2C3D4` \- the `regex_rules` field is a repeater rendered from the schema; each entry has `name`, `pattern`, optional `flags`, and an `entity` selector (same vocabulary as step 2). Patterns are compile-validated at save time. The administrator does *not* invent new entity classes \- `regex_rules` extends pattern coverage, not the vocabulary.  
     
5. **Set tool deanonymization policy.** Default is `mode: none` \- no tool ever sees real values. The administrator leaves it as-is. (If a specific workflow later needed a real-data tool \- e.g., an entity-analytics risk-score lookup that has to receive the actual user identifier \- the policy would be switched to `mode: allowlist` with that tool's ID listed.)  
     
6. **Save and register.** The workflow is saved. To activate it for every agent in the space, the administrator goes to **Stack Management → Advanced Settings**, searches for the pre-prompt-workflow-IDs setting, and adds the new workflow's ID. (For per-agent activation, the specific agent's `workflow_ids` configuration is edited instead.)  
     
7. **Verify.** The administrator opens an agent's chat surface and sends a test message containing an employee ID, then inspects the inference span trace (or APM/observability) and confirms the outgoing LLM payload contains `USER_NAME_<32-hex>` instead of `EMP-12345`. The assistant's reply, as displayed in the UI, contains the original `EMP-12345` \- the deanonymization round-trip is complete.

**The resulting YAML.** This is the entire configuration surface \- there is no Stack Management UI for anonymization, no profile saved-objects, no separate detection-rule editor. The form-based editor saves to YAML; this is what the file looks like on disk.

```
version: '1'
name: Acme PII Anonymization
description: Anonymizes PII before LLM calls; includes custom employee/resource IDs.
enabled: true
tags:
  - anonymization
  - agent-builder

# AB invokes this workflow by ID. Register it in the
# AGENT_BUILDER_PRE_PROMPT_WORKFLOW_IDS Advanced Setting (or in a specific
# agent's `workflow_ids`); AB calls it from inside its beforeAgent hook.

steps:
  - name: anonymise
    type: ai.pii
    with:
      input: "{{ event.message }}"

      # Built-in entity classes to detect.
      entities:
        - PER          # NER
        - ORG          # NER
        - LOC          # NER
        - EMAIL        # bundled regex
        - IP           # bundled regex
        - HOST_NAME    # bundled regex
        - USER_NAME    # bundled regex

      # NER backend. The value is an ML trained-model deployment ID (NOT
      # an _inference endpoint id - NER isn't an _inference task type).
      # Omit or set to null for regex-only mode (no NER call).
      ner_deployment_id: "elastic__distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-conll03-english"

      # User-authored regex rules - for organization-specific identifiers.
      # Each rule maps a pattern to one of the canonical entity classes.
      regex_rules:
        - name: acme_employee_id
          pattern: "EMP-\\d{5,7}"
          entity: USER_NAME
        - name: acme_resource_id
          pattern: "ACME-RES-[A-Z0-9]{8}"
          entity: RESOURCE_ID
          flags: "i"

      hmac_key: "{{ event.conversationSalt }}"

      tool_deanonymization:
        mode: none
```

The workflow has a single operative step. Its output (`forward`, `inverse`, `entities`, `tool_deanonymization`, `system_prompt_instruction?`) is the workflow's output \- AB reads it directly from the execution result via the existing `normalizeWorkflowOutput` path in `run_before_agent_workflows.ts`. No separate emit step is needed.

That's it. The administrator's job is done; everything from here is invisible to end users.

### 2.2 End-User Interaction (Chat Role)

**Context.** An end user (e.g., an SRE or analyst) interacts with the Agent Builder chat surface for day-to-day work. Anonymization is already configured for the space per §2.1.

**Steps.**

1. **Open the agent.** The user opens the Agent Builder chat surface. There is no anonymization toggle, no banner, no extra step \- the agent looks identical to one without anonymization.  
     
2. **Send a message containing PII.** The user types: *"What's the deployment status for John Smith's project (EMP-48217)? His email is [john.smith@acme.com](mailto:john.smith@acme.com)."* and sends.  
     
3. **Agent responds normally.** The reply streams in: *"John Smith (EMP-48217)'s deployment to staging completed 2h ago. Production rollout is on hold pending approval. I've drafted a summary for [john.smith@acme.com](mailto:john.smith@acme.com)."*  
     
4. **The user sees real values everywhere.** The name, the employee ID, and the email appear in the chat exactly as typed and as the agent describes them. The conversation history, when scrolled back, shows real values. Tool calls displayed in the UI (if any) also show real-valued params \- even for tools that internally received tokenized params, the user-visible representation is deanonymized.

**What the user does *not* see.**

* The token strings (`PER_a3f2…`, `USER_NAME_c8b1…`, `EMAIL_4e1d…`) the LLM actually saw and emitted. Those exist only in transit between AB and the LLM provider.  
* The conversation salt that makes tokens deterministic across turns.  
* The anonymization workflow's existence at all.

**What the user *might* notice.**

* \~50–150ms of additional delay before the agent starts streaming a response (the anonymization workflow runs first, before the LLM call). At those numbers it's well below the round's overall latency floor and unlikely to be perceptible (§4.4).  
    
* If anonymization fails (e.g., the ML node is unreachable and the workflow is configured with NER required), the agent surfaces a clear error \- *"Could not process message. Anonymization workflow failed."* \- rather than silently sending PII to the LLM. Fail-closed by design (§3.4).

**What the user *cannot* do (intentional).**

* Bypass anonymization for a specific message. If the workflow is registered, every round goes through it. To disable, a privileged user removes the workflow ID from the pre-prompt setting.  
    
* See or interact with tokens directly. They're internal infrastructure, not part of the user-facing UX.

The end-user experience is, by design, "AI agent works, my data doesn't leave the cluster in raw form, I don't have to think about it." The contrast with the administrator workflow is the whole point: configuration is explicit and YAML-driven; usage is invisible.

---

## 3\. Technical Architecture

### 3.1 Lifecycle Hooks \- what we use vs. what we add

Agent Builder ships three lifecycle hooks today (`x-pack/platform/packages/shared/agent-builder/agent-builder-common/hooks/lifecycle.ts:13-17`):

```ts
export enum HookLifecycle {
  beforeAgent      = 'beforeAgent',
  beforeToolCall   = 'beforeToolCall',
  afterToolCall    = 'afterToolCall',
}
```

Hooks are registered via `AgentBuilderPluginSetup.hooks.register(bundle)` (`x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/agent_builder/server/plugin.ts:253`) and run with priority ordering, blocking/nonBlocking modes, and a 2-minute default timeout (`hooks_runner.ts:25` \- note the JSDoc comment on that line says "5 minutes" but the value is 2 minutes; worth a docstring fix in passing). `afterToolCall` blocking handlers run in **reverse** priority order (inner-first unwinding) \- see `hooks_runner.ts:27,63-64`.

| Stage of round | Existing hook? | Use it for |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Before LLM ever sees the user's message | ✅ `beforeAgent` (`run_chat_agent.ts:160-166`) \- gives `{ nextInput: ProcessedRoundInput }`, can rewrite | **Run the anonymization workflow** to detect PII and populate the token map; `nextInput` itself is left as real values (see §3.2) |
| Before a tool call leaves the runner | ✅ `beforeToolCall` (`run_tool.ts:109`) \- gives `{ toolParams }`, can rewrite | **Deanonymize** tool params for allowlisted tools (the LLM produced tokens; allowlisted tools need originals) |
| After a tool returns | ✅ `afterToolCall` (`run_tool.ts:235`) \- gives `{ toolReturn }`, can rewrite, runs in reverse priority | **Re-anonymize** tool results so the LLM context never sees originals |

The LLM is called many times per round; `beforeAgent` is the once-per-round entry point we need. There is no `afterAgent` and we do not propose adding one \- the apparent asymmetry ("user sees real values, LLM does not") is resolved by wrapping the LLM I/O instead of the round (see §3.2).

### 3.2 Where deanonymization happens \- inference I/O wrapping, not a round hook

Anonymization is fundamentally an **inference-call concern**, not a round-boundary concern. The LLM is what we're hiding PII from; everywhere else (storage, the user, allowlisted tools) gets real values. If we wrap the LLM I/O instead of the round, there is nothing for an `afterAgent` hook to do.

Two transform points are introduced \- both **internal AB infrastructure**, neither a new public lifecycle:

| Transform | Where | What it does |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **transform-out** (forward) | An `AnonymizingChatModel` decorator class (lives in `kbn-anonymization`, composes any `InferenceChatModel` from `@kbn/inference-langchain`). AB never calls `inference.chatComplete()` directly \- every LLM call goes through `chatModel.bindTools(...).invoke(messages)` or `chatModel.invoke(messages)`. There are at least five such call sites today (graph.ts × 2, generate\_title.ts, answer\_agent\_structured.ts, conversation\_compactor.ts \- see §7). AB instantiates the decorator once per round (with that round's forward/inverse maps) and substitutes it for the inner model; every call site is covered uniformly. Consumers compose the decorator at the point they construct `InferenceChatModel` \- there is no automatic injection. It's a regular langchain decorator. | Replaces real values with tokens in the outgoing message list, using the round's `forward` map |
| **transform-in** (inverse) | On LLM-produced output before it emits to the chat event stream \- both natural-language chunks (`messageChunk` / `messageComplete` / `reasoning`) and tool-call structures (`toolCall` event params). `thinkingComplete` is intentionally excluded \- its `ThinkingCompleteEventData` carries only `time_to_first_token` and no text. The tool-call deanonymization here is *only* for the client/storage path; the LLM-context copy of tool calls (the path that flows into `beforeToolCall`) keeps tokens, and the existing allowlist asymmetry (allowlisted tools see real values via `beforeToolCall`, others see tokens) is unchanged. | Replaces tokens with real values, using `RunContext.anonymization.inverse` |

![][image1]

**Tool calls take two paths from the inference stream.** The LLM emits a tokenized tool-call. The fork is structural rather than literal \- the same tokenized payload ends up flowing through two distinct emission sites:

* **Tool execution path (decorator-internal, tokens preserved).** The `AnonymizingChatModel` decorator does not mutate `AIMessage.tool_calls` on the LangChain output. The tokenized tool-call flows through the runner into `beforeToolCall` (`run_tool.ts:109`) unchanged. The existing hook handles the allowlist asymmetry \- allowlisted tools receive deanonymized params (via the §3.4 `beforeToolCall` deanonymization step against `RunContext.anonymization.inverse`); other tools see tokens. `afterToolCall` (`run_tool.ts:235`) re-anonymizes results before they re-enter the LLM context.

* **Client/storage path (event-emitter side, deanonymized).** Tool-call chat events for the user-facing stream are produced by `createToolCallEvent({ params, … })` at `convert_graph_events.ts:141`. Right before that call (or in a thin wrapper around it), AB applies a recursive walk over `params` and looks each string leaf up in `RunContext.anonymization.inverse` \- own-property check, `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`. The user sees `emailSender(to: "john@acme.com", …)`, not `to: EMAIL_…`. Storage receives the same real-valued representation.

The decorator never mutates tool-calls; AB's event emitter applies inverse-map deanonymization to the user-facing copy. This separation keeps the §1 invariant true: the user never sees tokens in any natural-language or tool-call display; the LLM never sees real PII unless it routed through an explicitly allowlisted tool.

**Hallucinated tokens are safe.** The streaming buffer scans for token-shaped substrings (that's how candidates are extracted), but substitution only fires when a candidate is an exact own-property key in the inverse map (use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(inverse, token)` to avoid prototype-pollution surprises). If the LLM invents a token-shaped string that wasn't in our forward map (e.g., `EMAIL_unknown` or `PER_deadbeef00000000000000000000000`), the lookup misses and the string passes through unchanged. The user sees a confusing-looking string at worst \- never a PII leak via the wrong substitution.

**Storage policy.** With real values flowing through everywhere except inside the LLM call, conversation history is stored with originals. This matches the prior team consensus that anonymization is an LLM-edge concern, not a storage concern \- what we're hiding is data sent to external providers, not data sitting at rest in our own indices. It also drops the old design's encrypted-at-rest index and per-space key concerns entirely.

**Streaming.** Transform-in operates on the chunked stream with a fixed-size lookahead buffer to handle tokens that span chunk boundaries. Worst-case token length under the existing entity vocabulary (longest names `CLOUD_ACCOUNT` and `RESOURCE_NAME`, 13 chars each) plus `_` plus the 32-char hex suffix produced by `generateToken` (`DEFAULT_HASH_LENGTH = 32`, defined in `kbn-anonymization` per §7; carried over unchanged from the deprecated `anonymization-common` implementation) ≈ 46 bytes. We size the buffer at **256 bytes** to comfortably absorb (a) the longest expected token (\~46 bytes) and (b) chunk-boundary headroom from providers that flush single tokens at a time \- see §6.1 for cross-provider validation. Concretely: buffer the last N bytes of each emitted chunk, scan the joined `(buffer + new chunk)` for token-shaped substrings, look each candidate up in the inverse-map record (own-property check), emit the safely-resolved prefix, and retain the suffix as the new buffer until end-of-stream. The chat event stream emits already-deanonymized chunks; the client renders real values directly with no special-case handling.

### 3.3 Trigger chaining \- how the token map flows

We adopt **Alternative A** from the [talboren/workflows-aop](https://github.com/talboren/workflows-aop) draft proposal: the token map flows through caller-held memory. No persistent storage.

![][image2]

The token map lives on the per-round `RunContext` (existing type at `agent-builder-server/runner/runner.ts:96-105`, currently exposes `runId: string` and `stack: RunContextStackEntry[]`). We extend it with a typed `anonymization` slot:

```ts
// [PROPOSED extension to existing RunContext]
interface RunContext {
  runId: string;
  stack: RunContextStackEntry[];
  anonymization?: {
    forward: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;   // original → token
    inverse: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;   // token → original
    entities: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;  // token → entity type (for telemetry/UI affordances)
    toolDeanonymization: ToolDeanonymizationPolicy;
  };
}
```

Plain objects (not `Map`) are intentional: `RunContext` is documented as serializable (`runner.ts:91-95` \- *"Will be attached to errors thrown during a run. It is serializable."*) and is JSON-stringified in adjacent code paths (e.g., `safeJsonStringify` calls in `execute_workflow.ts:92, 121, 133, 141`). `Map` instances JSON-serialize to `{}`, which would silently drop the token map from logs and span attributes. The plain-object shape also matches what the existing detection code already produces (`get_entity_mask.ts`).

Both transforms (the LLM-call wrapper and the chat-event-stream rewrite) read the slot from the same `RunContext`. The two existing tool hooks read the slot too. No `replacementsId`, no ES round-trip. When the round ends and `RunContext` goes out of scope, the map is GC'd.

### 3.4 Tool call strategy

`beforeToolCall` and `afterToolCall` already exist. The anonymization integration registers a hook bundle with priority chosen to run after any other guardrail-style hooks but before tool execution.

**`beforeToolCall` (blocking):**

1. Read `RunContext.anonymization` \- return early if not set.  
2. Check `policy.toolDeanonymization` \- return early unless this tool is allowed.  
3. Recursively walk `toolParams`, replacing tokens with originals from the `inverse` map.  
4. Return `{ toolParams: deanonymized }`.

**`afterToolCall` (blocking):**

1. Read `RunContext.anonymization` \- return early if not set.

2. **Detect newly-introduced PII in `toolReturn.results`.** A tool can return values that weren't in the original user message (e.g., a security search returns names of unrelated users). Run the `ai.pii` step's detection logic against the serialized tool result text and add any newly-detected entities to `forward`/`inverse`/`entities` maps on `RunContext.anonymization`. The HMAC determinism guarantees stable tokens \- if the same value appeared in the user message and again in a tool result, both sites produce the same token automatically. This adds NER+regex cost per tool result; it is the price of closing the new-PII leak.

3. Recursively walk `toolReturn.results`, replacing originals with tokens using the now-extended `forward` map. Iterate the map keys in **descending length order** so that longer values are replaced before substrings of them (e.g., replace "Jane Smith" before "Jane" to avoid partial collisions). The same ordering rule applies to transform-out (§3.2).

4. Return `{ toolReturn: reanonymized }`.

**Substitution complexity.** Recursive walk \+ descending-length-keyed substitution is O(map\_size × content\_length) per pass, applied at transform-out (every LLM call), transform-in (chunked, every emission), and `afterToolCall` (every tool result). For long tool results crossed with large maps this is non-trivial; not a correctness concern but worth profiling alongside the latency measurement (§6.6). If it becomes the bottleneck, the natural optimization is an Aho–Corasick matcher built once per round.

The round-trip guarantee: real values may flow **into** an allowlisted tool, but they never flow **back out** into the LLM context.

**Failure mode.** Failure semantics differ across the three hooks and should not be conflated:

* **`beforeAgent` (anonymization workflow execution):** This is where the token map is built. A silent failure here means PII reaches the LLM unredacted, which is the worst possible outcome. The current `beforeAgent` workflow integration is **already fail-closed**: `runBeforeAgentWorkflows` throws `createWorkflowExecutionError` / `createWorkflowAbortedError` on every failure path (`run_before_agent_workflows.ts:102, 110, 130`), and as a blocking hook handler this aborts the round. We keep this behavior for the anonymization workflow. Whether to expose a `fail_closed: boolean` opt-out for *non-anonymization* workflows that may want log-and-proceed is tracked as an open question (§6.3); it would not change the default for anonymization.

* **`beforeToolCall` and `afterToolCall` (deanonymize/re-anonymize tool I/O):** If `RunContext.anonymization` is unset (because the upstream workflow aborted, or no anonymization workflow is registered), these hooks short-circuit and do nothing. If the deanonymize/re-anonymize transform itself throws (e.g., malformed token map), the tool call should be aborted with a user-visible error rather than letting the LLM see real values for a tool we didn't intend to allowlist. This is also fail-closed by intent.

### 3.5 Putting it together \- call flow

![][image3]

**Note on multiple LLM calls per round.** The runner may call inference several times (reasoning, tool decisions, final response). The transform-out / transform-in wrapper applies on every call uniformly \- the forward and inverse maps don't change mid-round.

### 3.6 Multi-workflow token map merging

Multiple workflows whose IDs appear in `AGENT_BUILDER_PRE_PROMPT_WORKFLOW_IDS` (or in an agent's per-agent `workflow_ids`) run in sequence on every round \- a security guardrail and an anonymization workflow might both be registered. AB already loops over the configured ID list (`run_before_agent_workflows.ts:91-135`); we extend it to merge each workflow's anonymization output before storing on `RunContext.anonymization`. The merge algorithm:

1. **Union all `forward`, `inverse`, and `entities` maps.** Determinism is what makes the union safe. The token-generation contract is `generateToken(salt, entityClass, field, value)` \- re-declared in `kbn-anonymization` with the same signature as the deprecated `anonymization-common` implementation (see §7); `field` is part of the hash input. To make cross-workflow union idempotent, the `ai.pii` step pins `field = entityClass` for natural-language detection (preserving the convention used by the deprecated detection code's fallback path). AB synthesizes the workflow event payload (passed as `workflowParams.event`, which `runWorkflow` destructures onto `context.event` \- see `workflows_management_api.ts:325-331`) and includes `event.conversationSalt`, so independent workflows that both detect "[john@acme.com](mailto:john@acme.com)" *and classify it as the same entity class* produce the identical HMAC token (and the union is idempotent for any such value). Workflow authors don't have to think about `field` \- the step always passes `entityClass`.  
     
2. **Reject class disagreements by aborting the round.** **Same value, different entity class:** if workflow A classifies "Acme Corp" as `ORG` and workflow B classifies it as `MISC`, the same source value produces two different tokens (`ORG_…` vs `MISC_…`). Both end up in `forward`, and substitution becomes order-dependent on object property insertion order. Detect this at merge time \- if any source value appears in two workflows' `forward` records with different tokens, abort the round with a user-visible error. Fail-closed: a partial/inconsistent union is worse than no anonymization.  
     
3. **`toolDeanonymization` policies use most-restrictive-wins.** If workflow A says `mode: allowlist` and workflow B says `mode: none`, the merged result is `mode: none`. Precedence: `none > allowlist > all`. For `allowlist` mode, the allowed tool IDs from all workflows are unioned (a tool allowed by any workflow is allowed).

This is a deliberate divergence from the old RFC's `Deny > Anonymize > Allow` field-level merge logic. In the new model, the only point of conflict is the tool deanonymization policy \- detection maps are purely additive when all workflows use the same HMAC strategy and salt.

### 3.7 System prompt instruction injection

When transform-out applies the forward map, the LLM will encounter token strings it has never seen before (e.g., `EMAIL_a3f2c1d809e64b275fae2a8c9b1d04e7`). Without context, the LLM may hallucinate what the tokens represent, attempt to "fill them in", or produce incoherent output.

AB **automatically** injects a short instruction into the system prompt on every LLM call where `RunContext.anonymization` is set. This is infrastructure-owned, not user-authored:

```
[System - Anonymization]
Some values in this conversation have been replaced with privacy tokens.
Tokens follow the pattern <ENTITY_TYPE>_<hex32> (e.g., EMAIL_a3f2c1d809e64b275fae2a8c9b1d04e7,
PER_c8b1f5e30a4d82179a3e7b6c4d8e102f, HOST_NAME_4e1d97aa20b8f3c9d5b2e7af14c63890).
Entity types come from a fixed canonical vocabulary (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC,
EMAIL, IP, HOST_NAME, USER_NAME, URL, …). The hex suffix is the first 32
hex characters (128 bits) of HMAC-SHA256 - wide enough that collisions are
negligible at any realistic scale.
Rules:
  - Preserve tokens exactly as written; do not attempt to guess or reveal the original value.
  - If asked to use a token in an action (e.g., send email to EMAIL_a3f2c1d809e64b275fae2a8c9b1d04e7),
    treat the token as the identifier - do not refuse on the grounds that it "looks like a placeholder".
  - Do not mention that anonymization is in effect unless the user asks directly.
```

The instruction is appended once per LLM call (transform-out happens on every call). It is generated dynamically from `RunContext.anonymization.entities` so it lists only the entity types actually present in this round.

**Token cost.** The default instruction is roughly 150 tokens. Multiplied across reasoning, tool-decision, and final-response calls within a single round (the runner can issue several inference calls \- see §3.5), this is a non-trivial recurring overhead per round. Worth measuring alongside the latency overhead (§6.6). If the cost becomes prohibitive, plausible mitigations are (a) ship a shorter instruction once per *session* via the system prompt rather than per call, or (b) cache the instruction text on `RunContext` and ship it only when the entity-type set changes within a round.

Workflow authors do not write or manage this instruction \- they get it for free. If they want to override the wording, they set `system_prompt_instruction` on the `ai.pii` step's input (it surfaces as an optional textarea in the schema-derived form); the step echoes it through to its output and AB uses it instead of the default.

---

## 4\. Workflow Components

### 4.1 Step definitions

We register two `BaseStepDefinition` entries (from `@kbn/workflows`, identical shape to the existing `ai.classify` / `ai.summarize` / `ai.prompt` definitions in `src/platform/plugins/shared/workflows_extensions/common/steps/ai/`) with the workflow engine. Each definition supplies:

- `id` (the step type ID, e.g. `'ai.pii'`) and `category: StepCategory.Ai` \- the palette uses these to surface the step under **AI**.  
- `label`, `description`, and `documentation.{details,examples}` (i18n strings) \- shown in the picker and the docs panel.  
- `inputSchema`, `outputSchema`, and (optionally) `configSchema` as Zod schemas \- drive runtime validation, type inference, and the schema-derived configuration form rendered by the Workflows editor (§2.1 step 1).

The exact registration host depends on the §4.2 ownership decision: under the recommended Option B, both step definitions live in a new `kbn-anonymization` package as factories (`createAiPiiStepDefinition({ regexExecutor }): BaseStepDefinition`, see §4.2) and are constructed and registered by Agent Builder's plugin during `setup()`. (For historical context, the deprecated PoC ran detection through illustrative `anonymize_fields` / `anonymize_content` steps registered by the to-be-removed anonymization plugin; the new design replaces both with a single `ai.pii` step.)

**`ai.pii`** \- runs detection on natural-language text, returns the anonymized rewrite plus the token maps. Pure function; bundled and user-authored regex rules run on the same Piscina worker pool to avoid blocking the Kibana event loop (see §4.2).

```ts
interface AiPiiInput {
  /** The natural-language text to scan. In AB workflows this is bound to `event.message`
   *  (the textual content of every message in the round's outgoing LLM context, plus the
   *  new user message — see §4.1). */
  input: string;

  /** Entity classes to detect, drawn from `ANONYMIZATION_ENTITY_CLASSES`
   *  (e.g. `PER`, `ORG`, `EMAIL`, `IP`, `HOST_NAME`). NER-eligible classes are routed to
   *  the trained-model deployment; the rest are matched by bundled regex. */
  entities: EntityType[];

  /** HMAC key for token generation. In AB workflows this is bound to `event.conversationSalt`
   *  (§5.2); workflow authors do not pick this value. Token generation is HMAC-SHA256 only —
   *  determinism is load-bearing for the no-persistent-storage property (§5.2). */
  hmac_key: string;

  /** ML trained-model deployment ID for NER. `null` or omitted → regex-only mode (always safe).
   *  NER is *not* an `_inference` task type — see §4.2. */
  ner_deployment_id?: string | null;

  /** User-authored regex patterns, each mapped to one of the canonical entity classes
   *  (no new vocabulary is invented here; see §4.2). */
  regex_rules?: Array<{
    name: string;
    pattern: string;
    flags?: string;
    entity: EntityType;
  }>;

  /** Per-tool deanonymization policy applied at `beforeToolCall` (§3.4). Default `{ mode: 'none' }`. */
  tool_deanonymization?: ToolDeanonymizationPolicy;
}

interface AiPiiOutput {
  /** The input text with detected entities replaced by tokens. */
  anonymized_text: string;

  /** Real value → token. Used by transform-out (§3.2) on outgoing LLM messages. */
  forward: Record<string, string>;

  /** Token → real value. Used by transform-in (§3.2) on LLM responses and by the
   *  client/storage path on tool-call event params. */
  inverse: Record<string, string>;

  /** Token → entity class label, for the system-prompt instruction (§3.7) and observability. */
  entities: Record<string, EntityType>;

  /** Effective tool-deanonymization policy (echoed from input, defaulted if omitted). */
  tool_deanonymization: ToolDeanonymizationPolicy;

  /** Optional override for the default system-prompt instruction (§3.7). */
  system_prompt_instruction?: string;
}
```

**`transform.pii_restore`** \- pure function, provided for ad-hoc use inside other workflows (e.g. a workflow author wants to deanonymize a value before passing it to a notification step). Not part of the AB anonymization round-trip \- that is handled by transform-in (§3.2).

```ts
interface PiiRestoreInput {
  /** Tokenized text to restore. */
  input: string;

  /** Token → real value. Typically the `inverse` map produced by an earlier `ai.pii` step. */
  token_map: Record<string, string>;
}

interface PiiRestoreOutput {
  /** Input text with every token replaced by its real value (tokens not in the map pass through). */
  restored_text: string;
}
```

Both are stateless \- no DB writes, no I/O beyond NER inference. Workflow engine remains agnostic about what they do.

**Workflow output \= last step's output.** There is no `workflow.output` / emit step in this design. The Workflows engine returns the last operative step's output as the execution result, and `runBeforeAgentWorkflows` already normalizes and reads it via `normalizeWorkflowOutput(execution.output)` (`run_before_agent_workflows.ts:45-55, 117`). For an anonymization workflow whose only operative step is `ai.pii`, the step's output (`forward`, `inverse`, `entities`, `tool_deanonymization`, `system_prompt_instruction?`) flows through unchanged. AB extends `BeforeAgentWorkflowOutput` to include those fields and stores them on `RunContext.anonymization` (§3.3). Multi-step workflows that chain another step *after* `ai.pii` would need the last step to forward those fields explicitly \- but the common case (single `ai.pii` step) requires zero plumbing.

**Reusable beyond Agent Builder.** `ai.pii` is a generic workflow step. Any workflow \- a Cases automation that summarizes alerts, a Dashboard background job that titles ML jobs, a third-party plugin's audit pipeline \- can call it directly to get back a token map and an anonymized text. What's *AB-specific* in this RFC is only the transparent round-trip: the `RunContext.anonymization` slot, the `AnonymizingChatModel` decorator (also reusable, lives in `kbn-anonymization`), the system-prompt injection, and the per-round invocation in the `beforeAgent` hook. None of that is required to use the step itself. If a non-AB feature wants PII scrubbing, the entry cost is "register the workflow ID and call it" \- same as any other workflow.

**Scope of `input`.** The `ai.pii` step processes **natural-language text**. It is not a structured-JSON scrubber. This is intentional: NER and regex pattern matching are designed for prose; applying them to serialized JSON paths risks false positives (e.g., a short hostname matching a name pattern) and false negatives (regex anchors break on JSON escaping). Path-based structured field scrubbing (e.g., "anonymize `host.name` values in ES documents before sending to the LLM") is explicitly out of scope per the Slack consensus on field-level masking \- see §4.5. The transform-out pass (§3.2) applies the already-built token map across the full serialized outgoing message via exact-string replacement \- no regex re-scanning at that point, so no false-positive risk there either.

The step's `input` is `event.message` from the workflow event payload. AB constructs the round's outgoing LLM context first (existing logic, including any conversation compaction), then passes the textual content of every message in that context \- concatenated with the new user message \- as `event.message` (see §4.4). The HMAC-determinism guarantees that re-detecting the same value on a later round produces the same token without any persistent map.

**History-inclusion policy.** The detection window equals the LLM-visible window this round, **by construction**. Concretely: `event.message` is built from the textual content of every message AB will include in the round's outgoing LLM context \- user messages, tool-result text, *and* assistant/summary text \- plus the new user message. This is what makes the §3.2 invariant ("LLM never sees a real-valued PII string that isn't in the round's `forward` map") true regardless of how AB evolves its context-construction or compaction logic. Including assistant text is correct and cheap by HMAC determinism: re-running detection on already-tokenized-then-deanonymized assistant content reproduces the same tokens. Detection cost scales with the LLM context window, bounded by whatever the conversation compactor already bounds it to \- no separate knob, nothing for workflow authors to reason about.

### 4.2 NER \+ RegEx \- where the detection logic lives, and security requirements

**Backend is a trained model deployment, not an inference endpoint.** NER is *not* an Elasticsearch `_inference` task type \- `InferenceTaskType` is fixed at `'sparse_embedding' | 'text_embedding' | 'rerank' | 'completion' | 'chat_completion'`. NER detection is performed via the trained models API (`POST _ml/trained_models/{deployment_id}/_infer`), which is exactly the call path the deprecated implementation already uses (`x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/inference/server/chat_complete/anonymization/execute_ner_rule.ts:135` \- `esClient.ml.inferTrainedModel({ model_id, docs, … })`). The `ai.pii` step therefore takes a `ner_deployment_id` (trained-model deployment ID), not an `inference_id`.

**This is an open question that affects step ownership.** The deprecated rollout's NER and regex-worker code lives in `x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/inference/server/chat_complete/anonymization/` \- including `execute_ner_rule.ts` (created 2025-07-07), `regex_worker_service.ts` (created 2025-07-11), and `resolve_overlaps_and_mask.ts` (created 2025-08-21). All of this is recent code from the rollout, not legacy infrastructure. The plan calls for **surgical reverts** in the inference plugin rather than a clean delete because some non-anonymization inference functionality was added in the same period; we need to decide what the new home for NER \+ RegEx execution is:

- **Option A:** Keep the regex worker pool and NER execution code in the inference plugin (whatever survives the surgical revert) and have the `ai.pii` step call into it via the inference server contract.

- **Option B:** Move the worker code into a new package owned by Agent Builder (or a new `kbn-anonymization` package) so anonymization is fully self-contained and the inference plugin reverts cleanly.

- **Option C:** Embed detection directly in the step handler.

Recommended: **Option B** \- clean separation. The inference plugin reverts to its pre-anonymization shape; anonymization becomes an AB-side concern, consistent with "scope is AB only". The deletion of the deprecated `anonymization` plugin and the surgical reverts in the inference plugin and `gen_ai_settings` are tracked separately and are not the subject of this RFC; the only intersection is that some pre-existing worker-thread code may move along with Option B.

**Security requirement: NER must run within a trusted boundary.**

Sending raw text to an external LLM for NER detection in order to anonymize it before sending to that *same* LLM is circular and provides no security. The NER model must not be the same endpoint (or same provider session) as the agent's inference target.

**Selected NER model: `elastic__distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-conll03-english`.** This is the Elastic-maintained DistilBERT model fine-tuned on CoNLL-03, deployed on ES ML nodes via Eland. It runs fully locally \- no data leaves the cluster. This satisfies the trust boundary requirement by construction: the model runs in-cluster, distinct from any external LLM connector.

The `ai.pii` step's `ner_deployment_id` field defaults to this model's deployment ID. If no `ner_deployment_id` is supplied, the step falls back to pure regex detection (no NER), which is always safe. Note: the `NER_MODEL_ID` constant currently lives in `x-pack/platform/packages/shared/ai-infra/anonymization-common/src/schemas.ts:12` \- a package marked for deletion. Its new home is the proposed `kbn-anonymization` package (Option B below).

**NER vs regex coverage.** The CoNLL-03 model emits only four classes: `PER, ORG, LOC, MISC` (`anonymization-common/src/schemas.ts:17`). All other entity types (`EMAIL`, `IP`, `HOST_NAME`, `USER_NAME`, `URL`, `CLOUD_ACCOUNT`, `ENTITY_NAME`, `RESOURCE_NAME`, `RESOURCE_ID`) come from regex rules. Per the existing convention there is no `PHONE` class \- phone-number-like text falls under `MISC`. Workflow authors specify entity *types* in the `entities:` list and the step routes each type to either NER or its bundled regex rule automatically.

**User-authored regex rules.** Workflow authors can add their own patterns via the step's `regex_rules` input \- useful for organization-specific identifiers (employee IDs, internal resource IDs, custom case-number formats). Each rule has the shape `{ name: string, pattern: string, flags?: string, entity: AnonymizationEntityClass }` and maps custom matches into the canonical entity vocabulary (the user picks which existing class their match belongs to \- they do not invent new classes). User-authored patterns run on the same Piscina worker pool as the bundled patterns, so a pathological pattern (catastrophic backtracking, unbounded lookahead) cannot block the Kibana event loop. At workflow-save time the step does basic sanity checks: pattern compiles under `RegExp`, `entity` is in `ANONYMIZATION_ENTITY_CLASSES`. Match results from user-authored rules flow through the same `resolve_overlaps_and_mask` layer as bundled-rule matches, so duplicates and overlaps are deduped consistently.

**Disabling NER.** Setting `ner_deployment_id` to `null` (or omitting the field) puts the step in regex-only mode \- it skips the NER call entirely and relies on bundled \+ user-authored regex rules. This is the right choice for environments without a deployed NER model, or when the user wants graceful degradation if the ML node is unavailable. Always safe by construction.

The vocabulary deliberately excludes domain-specific entities like `US_SSN`, `CREDIT_CARD`, and a dedicated `PHONE` class. If a future workflow needs them, the regex rule and the constant are added as a small follow-up \- the convention to preserve (`anonymization-common/src/schemas.ts:23-25`) is "compact/canonical, phone-like patterns use `MISC`." Until then, users can detect SSN/credit-card-shaped text by adding `regex_rules` and mapping them to `MISC`.

**Enforcement of the trust boundary.** The trust property we want is *"the configured NER backend is not the agent's LLM connector"* \- provider-agnostic. The `ai.pii` step does not have direct knowledge of which agent is currently running, so it cannot itself compare its `ner_deployment_id` to the agent's LLM connector ID. The runtime guard does the actual work; the registration-time check is a best-effort early warning.

1. **Runtime guard in the step executor (load-bearing).** Every time the step executes, it resolves `ner_deployment_id` against the ML trained models registry; the deployment must exist and (when interrogable) advertise a token-classification task. As a defence-in-depth check, the guard also rejects any value that resolves to an `_inference` endpoint of `task_type: chat_completion` (in case a workflow author misuses `ner_deployment_id` to point at a chat-completion endpoint id). This works even if endpoints are added or reconfigured after the workflow was registered.

2. **Static validation at workflow registration (best-effort).** When a workflow is registered as a pre-prompt workflow (added to `AGENT_BUILDER_PRE_PROMPT_WORKFLOW_IDS` or to an agent's `workflow_ids`), AB checks that any `ai.pii` step's `ner_deployment_id` is not currently in the set of registered LLM connector IDs. This catches typos and obvious misconfigurations at registration time, but it is **not a security boundary** \- a connector with the same ID as the NER deployment can be added after registration (TOCTOU). The runtime guard above is what closes that gap.

3. **Editor affordance (UX, not security).** The schema-derived form for the `ai.pii` step renders `ner_deployment_id` as a selector populated from the cluster's deployed ML trained models (the same registry surfaced by `x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/ml`). Whether to also surface the small set of `_inference` endpoints that wrap a token-classification ML model is a follow-up decision; the default is the trained-models list. This eliminates the typo class of failure for the form path; YAML edits that bypass the form still go through (1) and (2).

Both checks rest on the ML trained models registry being the authoritative source for "is this a deployed NER model" \- there is no NER task type in the `_inference` API to filter against.

For completeness, the broader hierarchy of acceptable NER backends:

1. **ES ML nodes / Eland model** \- fully local, no data leaves the cluster. Accessed via `_ml/trained_models/{deployment_id}/_infer`. (**selected**)  
2. **A custom token-classification ML model deployed by the customer** (e.g., a domain-specific PHI model) \- same access path; the only requirement is "not the agent's LLM connector."  
3. **A different external provider** \- acceptable if the user consciously separates detection from inference, but not the default; the trust property is unchanged ("not the agent's LLM connector").

**Worker threads for regex execution.**

The deprecated implementation used a Piscina worker-thread pool (`regex_worker_service.ts`) to run regex rules off the main event loop. This must be preserved in the new `ai.pii` implementation. A heavy regex rule (e.g., a complex multi-line pattern against a large message) must not block Kibana's main event loop. Worker threads are a hard implementation requirement, not an optimisation.

**Pool ownership (lifecycle).** Packages do not have plugin lifecycles, so the worker pool cannot be a singleton inside `kbn-anonymization` \- workers would leak across plugin restarts in dev and we'd have nowhere to call `pool.destroy()`. The package therefore exports two factories rather than a runtime resource:

- `createRegexWorkerPool(opts: { size: number; timeoutMs: number }): RegexExecutor` \- constructs the pool. The caller owns its lifecycle.  
- `createAiPiiStepDefinition({ regexExecutor: RegexExecutor, /* …other deps */ }): BaseStepDefinition` \- constructs the step definition with an injected executor.

Agent Builder's plugin calls `createRegexWorkerPool(...)` in `start()`, owns the returned `RegexExecutor` (calling `destroy()` in `stop()`), and passes it into `createAiPiiStepDefinition(...)` when registering the step with the workflow engine. The package stays pure (no runtime resources, no lifecycle assumptions); the plugin owns lifecycle. If a non-AB consumer adopts the step in the future, they construct their own pool the same way \- yes, that means duplication if both consumers are simultaneously active, but in practice AB is the only consumer for the foreseeable future, and the alternative (a package singleton with no shutdown) trades that theoretical duplication for real worker leaks.

**Failure modes by component.** The system is fail-closed by structure \- every error path aborts the round before any PII reaches the LLM. Each component's failure mode is bounded:

| Failure | What happens | Operator knob |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Workflow engine error (engine down, definition invalid) | `executeWorkflow` returns `success: false` → `runBeforeAgentWorkflows` throws → round aborts with user-visible error. | None \- engine has to be available. |
| `ai.pii` step throws (any reason: NER call failed, regex worker timed out, malformed input) | Step error → workflow status `FAILED` → `runBeforeAgentWorkflows` throws → round aborts. | Omit `ner_deployment_id` to skip NER (regex-only path; reduces dependency on ML node). |
| ML node down or NER deployment unavailable | NER call inside `ai.pii` throws → falls through to step-throws case above. | Same as above. The user can configure a regex-only workflow as a graceful-degradation path. |
| Regex worker pool exhausted / Piscina queue overflow | Step throws or times out → round aborts. | Worker pool size is configurable in `ai.pii` step config. |
| Token map malformed (empty `forward`, missing `inverse`) | `RunContext.anonymization` is unset → tool hooks short-circuit (no deanonymization), transform-out passes messages through unchanged → LLM sees real PII. | This is the one case worth a runtime assertion: validate map shape before storing on `RunContext`; if invalid, abort the round. |
| Transform throws inside a tool hook (malformed token in tool output) | `beforeToolCall` / `afterToolCall` throws → tool call is aborted with a user-visible error. | None \- better to fail visibly than to leak. |

There is no "fail-open" default for anonymization. The closest knob is to omit `ner_deployment_id` so the workflow can run without the ML node \- that's a graceful-degradation path, not a fail-open.

**Bring your own NER.** The `ner_deployment_id` field accepts any deployed ML trained model that exposes the standard token-classification inference shape. A customer with a domain-specific model (e.g., a medical NER model fine-tuned for PHI) deploys it via Eland and points `ner_deployment_id` at it. The trust-boundary checks above apply to all backends \- the load-bearing requirement is "not the agent's LLM connector." This is a real platform extension point, not a marketing claim.

**ECS entity-class smart defaults (out of scope here).**

The old RFC included an `ECS_ENTITY_CLASS_MAP` (in the deprecated `anonymization-common/src/ecs_entity_class_suggestions.ts`) that automatically inferred the entity class from a field name (e.g., `host.name` → `HOST_NAME`, `source.ip` → `IP`). In the NER-on-text model used here, the user specifies entity *types* (e.g., `PER`, `IP`) not field paths \- so the old map doesn't apply. The map only becomes relevant if a future proposal adds path-based structured field scrubbing (which is explicitly out of scope per §4.5). The constant is dropped along with `anonymization-common`; if path-based scrubbing is later proposed, the map can be recovered from git history or rebuilt from the ECS schema.

### 4.3 Configuration \- by-value, in YAML

A single workflow file is the entire configuration surface. No Stack Management UI, no profile saved-objects.

```
version: '1'
name: Agent Builder PII Anonymization
description: >
  Anonymizes user messages before they reach the LLM and configures
  which tools may receive deanonymized parameters.
enabled: true
tags:
  - anonymization
  - agent-builder

# AB invokes this workflow by ID. Register it in the
# AGENT_BUILDER_PRE_PROMPT_WORKFLOW_IDS UI setting (or in a specific agent's
# `workflow_ids`); AB calls it from inside its beforeAgent hook handler via
# executeWorkflow({waitForCompletion: true}) - see §4.4.
# Per-agent filtering happens at registration time (the workflow ID lives on
# the agent), not via a YAML condition.

steps:
  - name: anonymise
    type: ai.pii                              # [PROPOSED STEP]
    with:
      input: "{{ event.message }}"

      # Built-in entity classes detected.
      # NER classes (PER/ORG/LOC/MISC) are detected by the NER model below.
      # Domain classes (EMAIL/IP/HOST_NAME/etc.) are detected by bundled regex.
      entities:
        - PER          # NER: people
        - ORG          # NER: organisations
        - LOC          # NER: locations
        - MISC         # NER: catch-all (incl. phone-like patterns by convention)
        - EMAIL        # bundled regex
        - IP           # bundled regex
        - HOST_NAME    # bundled regex
        - USER_NAME    # bundled regex
        - URL          # bundled regex

      # NER backend. The value is an ML trained-model deployment ID accessed
      # via _ml/trained_models/{id}/_infer (NER is NOT an _inference task
      # type). Omit or set to `null` for regex-only mode (no NER call;
      # bundled + user-authored regex only).
      ner_deployment_id: "elastic__distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-conll03-english"

      # User-authored regex rules - for organization-specific identifiers
      # not covered by the bundled patterns. Each rule maps custom matches
      # into the canonical entity vocabulary (no new entity classes).
      # Patterns run on the same Piscina worker pool as bundled rules,
      # so a heavy pattern can't block the Kibana event loop.
      regex_rules:
        - name: acme_employee_id
          pattern: "EMP-\\d{5,7}"
          entity: USER_NAME
        - name: acme_resource_id
          pattern: "ACME-RES-[A-Z0-9]{8}"
          entity: RESOURCE_ID
          flags: "i"

      # The HMAC key is the per-conversation salt. AB synthesizes the workflow
      # event payload (passed via workflowParams.event, which runWorkflow
      # destructures onto context.event - see workflows_management_api.ts:325)
      # and includes `event.conversationSalt`. Workflow authors do not pick
      # this value - a workflow-constant secret would defeat per-conversation
      # isolation.
      hmac_key: "{{ event.conversationSalt }}"

      # Default policy is `mode: none` - no tool ever sees real values.
      # Listing tool_ids is the exceptional case (a security-analyst workflow
      # that needs to call a real-data tool); most workflows omit
      # tool_deanonymization entirely and use the safe default.
      tool_deanonymization:
        mode: allowlist                        # 'allowlist' | 'all' | 'none'; default 'none'
        tool_ids:
          - 'security.entity_analytics.risk_score'
```

The `ai.pii` step is the only operative step. Its output (`forward`, `inverse`, `entities`, `tool_deanonymization`, `system_prompt_instruction?`) is the workflow's output \- see §4.1, "Workflow output \= last step's output." AB reads it from the execution result and stores it on `RunContext.anonymization`. There is no separate emit step.

`nextInput` is **not** rewritten by this workflow. Per §3.2, anonymization is applied at the LLM I/O boundary, not at the round boundary \- `nextInput` flows through unchanged with real values. AB stores the workflow's output on `RunContext.anonymization` and applies the transforms at the inference invocation sites.

There is no `afterAgent` workflow. Deanonymization happens transparently inside the runner (transform-in on text/reasoning chunks); workflow authors do not need to wire a second workflow for it. The `transform.pii_restore` step is provided for one-off scenarios where a workflow author wants to deanonymize a value explicitly inside another workflow \- it is not part of the AB anonymization round-trip.

### 4.4 How AB invokes the workflow

AB invokes the anonymization workflow by ID using the existing pattern at `x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/agent_builder/server/hooks/agent_workflows/run_before_agent_workflows.ts`: it iterates over the configured workflow ID list (from `AGENT_BUILDER_PRE_PROMPT_WORKFLOW_IDS` plus per-agent `workflow_ids`) and calls `executeWorkflow({ waitForCompletion: true })` for each. The integration adds two extensions to the existing call site:

1. **Pass `workflowParams.event = { message, conversationSalt, agentId, … }`** so the YAML's `{{ event.X }}` template paths resolve correctly. `runWorkflow` destructures the `event` key onto `context.event` (`workflows_management_api.ts:325-331`), so this works without any engine changes. The `message` field is *not* just the new user message \- it is the new message concatenated with the textual content of every message in the round's outgoing LLM context (per §4.1's history-inclusion policy: detection window \= LLM-visible window, by construction). This is what closes the cross-round PII gap: any PII the LLM is about to see this round is in the forward map by construction, and HMAC-deterministic re-detection produces the same token across rounds. From the step's perspective it's just a string.

2. **Read the workflow's anonymization output** (`forward`, `inverse`, `entities`, `toolDeanonymization`) from the execution result and store it on `RunContext.anonymization`. This requires extending `BeforeAgentWorkflowOutput` (currently `{abort?, abort_message?, new_prompt?}` at `hooks/agent_workflows/types.ts:14-18`) with the new fields.

The workflows engine also exposes an event-driven trigger model (`registerTriggerDefinition` \+ `emitEvent` in `src/platform/plugins/shared/workflows_extensions/server`), but `emitEvent` is fire-and-forget today \- `emit_event.ts:28` declares `export async function emitEvent(params, deps): Promise<void>` with no result and no synchronous semantics. We need a synchronous result (the token map) before the LLM call begins, so direct ID-based invocation is what we use. If the workflows engine later grows synchronous trigger invocation (e.g., the [talboren/workflows-aop](https://github.com/talboren/workflows-aop) draft proposal), AB can adopt it without changing the workflow contract \- but that's an internal AB change, out of scope here.

**Latency \- fast path.** The default polling cadence in `execute_workflow.ts:21-23` (1-second initial wait, 2.5-second polls, 120-second timeout) was tuned for general-purpose workflows that take seconds to minutes. For an `ai.pii` step that completes in tens of milliseconds it is wildly miscalibrated \- we'd be paying \~1 second of artificial wait for \~50ms of actual work. Two complementary fast-paths address this:

1. **Parameterize the polling cadence at the call site.** We extend `executeWorkflow` to accept overrides for `initialWaitMs` and `checkIntervalMs` \- currently module-scoped constants at `execute_workflow.ts:21-23` \- and pass `{ initialWaitMs: 0, checkIntervalMs: 50 }` from AB's anonymization invocation. Other callers keep the existing defaults. The change is \~10 lines (signature \+ plumbing); see §7. **Target budget** for a \~50ms workflow under this cadence is one or two `getExecutionState` polls against ES (\~50–150ms), to be validated per §6.6.  
     
2. **Single-step bypass.** Most anonymization workflows will be a single `ai.pii` step. At hook execution time, AB inspects the workflow definition; if it has exactly one operative step and that step is `ai.pii`, AB extracts the step config and runs it directly via the package's `createAiPiiStepDefinition` factory. The engine is skipped entirely \- overhead reduces to NER \+ regex execution time (a single ML node round-trip plus regex worker dispatch). Multi-step workflows (e.g., a security guardrail chained with anonymization) fall back to (1)'s engine path with the tightened cadence. The bypass path emits the same telemetry shape as the engine path so observability is unchanged.

**Future optimization (engine-side).** The right architectural answer is a completion notification on the engine side \- `executeWorkflow` returns a Promise that resolves on terminal status, or accepts an `onComplete` callback the engine emits when execution finishes. This eliminates polling entirely (sub-10ms wakeup latency). It needs a small workflows-engine PR (one method addition, one internal emit). AB would adopt it invisibly when it lands; the call-site contract here doesn't change. Out of scope for this RFC but worth pursuing in parallel.

**Practical impact (target, not measured).** With the fast-path in place, the anonymization step targets \~50ms in the common case (single-step bypass) and \~50–150ms in the chained-workflow case (parameterized polling). These are budgets to validate per §6.6, not measurements; the engine path also depends on `runWorkflow` scheduling latency and the bypass path on ML-node round-trip variance. The numbers are intended to stay well below baseline LLM round duration on any realistic agent.

### 4.5 What we are NOT proposing for this round

- A `tool_deanonymization` declaration in **tool registration** would be cleaner long-term but couples tool authoring to anonymization knowledge \- the workflow YAML stays the source of truth, and `mode: none` is the safe default so most workflows never touch the field. If we later want tool-side declaration, it's an additive change and a separate proposal.

- The `attachment_anonymizations` / `effectiveFieldPolicy` channels from the deprecated PoC. Removed during prior iteration; not in scope here.

- An **`anonymize_fields` step** for path-based structured JSON scrubbing. The `ai.pii` step processes natural-language text only (see §4.1). Path-based structured field scrubbing (e.g., anonymize the value at `host.name` in a tool result JSON blob) is **explicitly out of scope** per the prior team consensus that anonymization is an LLM-edge concern, not a storage or field-level concern. If a real use case appears, it's a separate proposal with its own design (path traversal, ECS smart defaults, collision rules).

- A registry of pre-built workflow templates. Authors copy the example YAML.

---

## 5\. State & Persistence

### 5.1 Session-based mapping

The token map is **request-scoped** \- it lives on `RunContext` for the duration of a single chat round and is GC'd when the round ends. Every consumer in a round (transform-out, transform-in, the two tool hooks) reads from the same `RunContext.anonymization` slot. The whole round runs on a single Kibana node under one `runId`, so distribution and concurrency are non-issues.

### 5.2 Multi-turn consistency via deterministic tokens

The architecture in §3 works **without** persistent token storage because two design choices remove the need for it:

1. **Storage holds real values** (per §3.2). Conversation history is stored deanonymized. There is nothing to "decode back" when a session is restored \- the stored content is already in the canonical form.  
2. **Tokens are HMAC-deterministic.** `ai.pii` uses `HMAC-SHA256(value, conversation_salt)` to generate tokens. The same input produces the same token deterministically. On turn 2, `jsmith` produces the same token it did on turn 1, even though the in-memory map from turn 1 is gone.

**Why HMAC and not a counter (`PERSON_1`, `PERSON_2`, …)?** The naïve counter approach forces persistent state: turn 1 assigns `PERSON_1=jsmith`; turn 2 has to remember that mapping, otherwise it either re-uses `PERSON_1` for someone else or starts again from `PERSON_1`. Either way, multi-turn consistency requires a stored counter and a stored mapping. HMAC sidesteps both \- the same input deterministically produces the same token on every turn, so we get consistency without persistence. The only thing we have to keep stable is the salt that seeds the HMAC.

The only persistent state required is the **conversation salt** \- a per-conversation random value stored alongside the conversation record. Without it, tokens would either (a) leak information across conversations if a global salt were used, or (b) be inconsistent across turns if regenerated per turn. The salt is one opaque string per conversation; it lives on AB's existing Conversation document (AB persists conversations directly in Elasticsearch via `ConversationService`, not as a SavedObject). Whether the field can be added to the existing index mapping in place or requires a version-bump/reindex is tracked as an open question (§6.2).

**What we explicitly do NOT introduce.** No new EncryptedSavedObject type. No salts service. No per-space encryption-key rotation. No `xpack.anonymization.active` feature flag. No `.kibana-anonymization-replacements` index. The only persistent artifact is one column on the existing conversation document. This is a deliberate reduction from the deprecated design's persistence story.

| Concern | Handled by |
| :---- | :---- |
| Where the map is allocated | `beforeAgent` hook stores `RunContext.anonymization` after the workflow returns |
| Where it's read | transform-out, transform-in, `beforeToolCall`, `afterToolCall` |
| When it's freed | Automatic \- Node GC's `RunContext` when the round resolves |
| Multi-turn token stability | Deterministic HMAC with the conversation's stable salt |
| Cross-session restore | Not needed \- storage is real values, retokenized on next turn |
| Distribution / concurrency | Round runs on a single node; conversation salt is durable |

This sidesteps every concern raised in the deprecated design's persistence story: no encrypted-at-rest replacements index, no per-space encryption keys, no `xpack.anonymization.active` feature flag, no migration story. The only durable artifact is one extra string per conversation.

**Why per-conversation scope is correct (not per-space).**

The old RFC used a per-space salt stored in an Encrypted Saved Object to achieve cross-conversation token consistency. That choice made sense in a model where stored messages were in anonymized form \- re-reading old messages required the same token map. In the new model, **storage holds real values**, which changes the calculus entirely.

Consider the cross-conversation scenario: "Remember the server from our last chat." When the user opens a new conversation, AB loads conversation history from storage as real values (e.g., "Server-A"). The `ai.pii` step in the new conversation detects "Server-A" and generates its token using the new conversation's salt \- a *different* token than turn 1 used. The LLM sees "Server-A" consistently represented by the new conversation's token throughout the new conversation. The user's question resolves correctly because the LLM is reasoning about the same retrieved real value (stored verbatim), not about a token from a previous conversation.

Cross-conversation token consistency would only matter if stored messages were in *tokenized* form \- that is the exact design we are rejecting. Per-conversation scope is the right choice for two practical reasons:

- **Isolation:** Token collisions between unrelated conversations are impossible. With a per-space salt, two conversations discussing "John Smith" produce the same token \- a user who can observe both conversations can infer they contain the same entity. Per-conversation salts make this inference impossible.  
- **Simplicity:** No encrypted saved objects, no per-space key rotation, no multi-tenant isolation concerns.

**The salt is not a confidentiality mechanism.** Worth being precise: the salt's job is cross-conversation isolation, not protecting the original values. To "reverse" a token, an attacker needs the salt *and* a candidate value to HMAC. Anyone who can read the salt (it sits next to the conversation in Elasticsearch) can almost certainly read the conversation's stored real-value content directly \- the salt does not gate access to PII; storage ACLs do. The narrower property the salt does provide: an attacker who intercepts in-flight LLM API traffic (e.g., at the provider, network logs) gets only token-shaped strings; reversing them requires the conversation's salt, which is scoped to that single conversation. That's a real but narrow defence. The salt is opaque, not secret.

### 5.3 Known limitation: cross-conversation token consistency

Tokens are consistent **within** a conversation but not **across** different conversations \- each conversation has its own salt. This has no observable effect today: storage holds real values, the LLM context is per-conversation, and tokens never reach the user. If a future feature requires cross-conversation tokens (e.g., a memory pattern that pipes tokenized output from one conversation into another without going through storage), the salt scope can be widened to per-user or per-space at that point. Out of scope here.

### 5.4 Memory considerations

A token map is three sibling `Record<string, string>` objects (forward, inverse, entities \- see §3.3). A worst-case round with 100 PII entities × \~64 bytes/entry × 3 records ≈ 20 KB. Negligible per round; bounded by the agent's own input/output size.

---

## 6\. Open Questions

These are real engineering TBDs that gate implementation. Each one needs to be confirmed before code lands.

1. **Streaming text rewriter validation.** §3.2 specifies a 256-byte lookahead buffer (worst-case \~46 bytes for the longest current entity name plus token suffix; padded for headroom). Worth validating against realistic chunk sizes from each LLM provider (OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex, etc.) to confirm the buffer doesn't introduce visible latency before the first user-visible chunk emits.

2. **Conversation salt provenance.** §5.2 requires one stable salt per conversation. New conversations generate one at creation; existing conversations need a lazy migration (generate on first use, no backfill required \- a missing salt simply means anonymization wasn't enabled for that conversation). AB persists conversations in Elasticsearch via `ConversationService`, not as Kibana SavedObjects, so the field is a mapping addition rather than a SavedObject migration. Confirm: (a) plaintext storage is acceptable (it is not a cryptographic secret, just an isolation key); (b) the index mapping update can ship without a reindex.

3. **Failure-mode opt-out for non-anonymization workflows.** Today's `beforeAgent` workflow integration is already fail-closed: `runBeforeAgentWorkflows` throws on every failure path (`run_before_agent_workflows.ts:102, 110, 130`) and the round aborts. For anonymization this is correct. The question is whether to expose a `fail_closed: boolean` field on the `ai.pii` step config (default `true`) as an opt-out for *non-anonymization* workflows that may want log-and-proceed semantics. A "no opt-out, ever" stance is also defensible. If we add the flag, confirm whether it belongs on the step or on the workflow registration.

4. **Reasoning chunk attachment.** §3.2 routes `messageChunk`, `messageComplete`, and `reasoning` through transform-in. Confirm reasoning chunks emit through the same path as text chunks in the inference plugin's stream \- if they don't, transform-in needs a second attachment point. (`thinkingComplete` is correctly excluded \- verified to carry no text payload.)

5. **System prompt instruction override UX.** §3.7 describes the automatic instruction injection with an optional `system_prompt_instruction` override on the `ai.pii` step (input field, echoed through to output). Confirm: (a) the field is optional in both the step's `inputSchema` and `outputSchema`; (b) AB falls back to the generated default if the field is absent on the workflow output; (c) the generated default wording should be reviewed by a UX writer before shipping, since it surfaces directly to the LLM's reasoning context.

6. **Round-duration overhead \- instrumentation.** §4.4's fast-path brings the worst case to \~150ms (chained workflows with tightened polling) and the common case to \~50ms (single-step bypass). The `afterToolCall` ai.pii pass (§3.4) and per-call instruction injection (§3.7) add further per-tool / per-call cost. Instrument typical and p95 round duration with anonymization on/off across representative agents to confirm the overhead matches expectations. This is a measurement task, not a product decision \- at the fast-path numbers there's no plausible regression scenario that would block shipping. If measurements come back materially worse (e.g., the engine-side bypass introduces unexpected ES read amplification), that informs whether to push harder on the engine-side completion-notification API (§4.4).

7. **Exposing the outgoing message list to `ai.pii`.** §4.1 ties detection scope to the round's outgoing LLM context: AB needs to construct the to-be-sent message list (or its textual content) *before* invoking the `beforeAgent` workflow, then pass it as `event.message`. Confirm: (a) `run_chat_agent.ts`'s current ordering (workflow runs at lines 160-166, before any of the five LLM call sites in §7) lets AB compute that context at that point; (b) intermediate steps within the round (researcher, tool calls, conversation compaction, title generation) that issue their own LLM calls don't see a *larger* set of textual content than what was passed to `event.message` \- if any do, `event.message` must be a superset, not just the answer-agent's view. The `afterToolCall` ai.pii pass (§3.4) already handles new entities introduced by tool results mid-round; this question is about whether any *pre-existing* content is reachable by an intra-round LLM call but not by `event.message`.

**Resolved during drafting:**

- ~~NER provider~~ \- `elastic__distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-conll03-english` deployed on ES ML nodes (§4.2), accessed via `_ml/trained_models/{id}/_infer`. Regex-only is the safe fallback when no `ner_deployment_id` is set.
